segments.title: Why North Carolina's vibration did not persist into later classes
segments.body: Correcting a defect already built into a ship is harder than preventing it in the next design. The original North Carolina-class ships remained difficult to fix. Once engineers understood the vibration source, they could remove it from the South Dakota and Iowa designs.

evidence.note: Why the vibration defect did not continue into the South Dakota and Iowa classes.

segments.summary: The North Carolina-class vibration problem was difficult to cure in the completed ships but could be removed from later designs.
segments.question: Did the vibration problems in Washington and North Carolina continue into the South Dakota and Iowa classes?
segments.answerShort: No. They were hard to fix once built into the North Carolinas, but understanding the problem allowed later designers to remove it.

segments.title: Would Resistance have formed a separate Revenge subclass?
segments.body: Resistance, Renown, and Repulse were planned as three further Revenges. Minor differences did not make them a separate Resistance subclass. If completed on that basis, they would perform the same duties as the other R-class battleships. A different construction decision could instead produce three battlecruisers along the lines of Renown and Repulse.

evidence.note: Resistance, Renown, and Repulse as planned Revenges, with a separate battlecruiser alternative.

segments.summary: Resistance, Renown, and Repulse were still planned as Revenge-class battleships; treating them as a separate slower subclass changes the premise.
segments.question: Would the proposed Resistance ships form a slower Revenge subclass used for convoy duties?
segments.answerShort: They were still Revenges and would perform the same duties. A substantially different alternative would be three Renown-style battlecruisers.

segments.title: When construction changes justify a subclass
segments.body: Royal Navy designs commonly changed as successive ships were built. Three Queen Elizabeth-class ships were slightly longer than the other two, but that difference did not make them a separate subclass. The Town-class examples involved new engines, different power ratings, and substantial internal rearrangement. A subclass therefore required a larger change than the small refinements expected during ordinary production.

evidence.note: Minor batch changes and the longer Queen Elizabeth examples.
Town-class subclasses distinguished by machinery, power, and internal rearrangement.

segments.summary: Slightly longer Queen Elizabeths illustrate batch changes, while the Town-class cruisers show the larger changes that justify subclasses.

segments.title: Why older capital ships would become treaty tonnage placeholders
segments.body: More surviving capital ships would probably bring only a modest increase in Britain's permitted tonnage at the Washington negotiations. The Royal Navy could keep the older ships as placeholders until replacement tonnage became available, then exchange them for new construction. Their value in this counterfactual would include protecting future building rights.

evidence.note: A larger British negotiating fleet, a possible increase in allowed tonnage, and the use of old ships as placeholders for later replacements.

segments.summary: Entering the Washington talks with more surviving battleships would probably secure only a slightly higher allowance, not freedom to retain them indefinitely.
segments.question: What changes if the Royal Navy enters the Washington negotiations with more surviving battleships and battlecruisers?
segments.answerShort: Probably only a somewhat larger tonnage allowance; the old ships would mainly serve as placeholders until Britain could replace them with new construction.

segments.title: Why ships from one class could differ between yards
segments.body: Ships ordered to the same design could acquire different dimensions during construction. Individual yards modified plans to suit their facilities and skills. In the Royal Navy, the Director of Naval Construction could approve or reject those changes and require the yard to retain the intended form. French yards had greater freedom to redesign a ship, helping explain the larger differences within some French classes.

evidence.note: Yard-specific modifications, British central approval, and greater French yard independence.

segments.summary: Yards adapted common designs to their facilities and methods, with central control limiting those changes more closely in the Royal Navy.

segments.title: Why foreign flag rank did not carry back into Royal Navy service
segments.body: A half-pay captain might become an admiral while organizing another country's fleet, but that foreign promotion did not alter his place in the Royal Navy. On return he would still be a captain, though the service could employ him as a commodore for a squadron or special duty. Commodore was historically an appointment signalled by a broad pennant rather than a permanent Royal Navy rank. An officer could therefore command as a commodore and still retire with the substantive rank of captain.

evidence.note: The foreign promotion does not transfer, although a returning captain might receive a broad pennant.
The broad pennant and the historical status of commodore as an appointment.

segments.summary: An officer returning from senior service abroad would retain his substantive Royal Navy rank, although he might receive a temporary broad pennant.
segments.question: Would a Royal Navy captain who became an admiral in a foreign navy return with that higher rank recognized?
segments.answerShort: No. He would still be a Royal Navy captain, although he might be appointed commodore for a particular command.

segments.title: Which of two Tigers would survive treaty reductions?
segments.body: The choice depends on the condition of the individual hull. A two-ship Tiger class would not guarantee that the original Tiger survived. The better-preserved ship would be the stronger candidate for retention.

evidence.note: Condition determines which of two hypothetical Tigers is retained.

segments.summary: In a hypothetical pair of Tiger-class battlecruisers, condition would determine which ship the Royal Navy retained.
segments.question: If there were two Tiger-class battlecruisers, which one would survive the treaty reductions?
segments.answerShort: Whichever ship was in the best condition.

segments.title: Why historians must keep each navy's class distinctions
segments.body: Navies did not all organize ships into classes in the same way. A difference too small to count as a Royal Navy subclass could still produce a separate class elsewhere. Historians moving between navies or periods therefore need to learn the relevant classification practice. They can criticize those distinctions, but should preserve the categories used by the navy they are studying.

evidence.note: Different navies and periods use different class boundaries.

segments.summary: A design difference that the Royal Navy treated as a variant could define a separate class in another navy.

segments.title: When Britain might leave an officer in an allied navy
segments.body: Utility and alliance politics would determine whether Britain left an officer in a foreign command. If the navy remained a useful ally, war did not automatically require his recall. The appointment could also give other British officers experience or help the ally operate its fleet. British officers serving aboard Russian ships show that such cross-navy service could be a practical wartime arrangement.

evidence.note: A useful allied posting could continue, as British officers' service aboard Russian ships illustrates.

segments.summary: A useful allied command could justify keeping a British officer in post and sending additional officers to learn from or support the arrangement.
segments.question: Would Britain leave an officer in command of a useful allied navy and use the post to train or employ more officers?
segments.answerShort: Yes, if the ally and assignment remained useful; British officers could stay and others might follow, as service aboard Russian ships illustrates.

segments.title: Why better navigation would not free sailing fleets from geography
segments.body: A French fleet with GPS would know its position more accurately, but it could not manoeuvre freely. Wind, tide, and current still restricted the routes sailing fleets could use and concentrated operations around predictable approaches. The Western Squadron's position off Brest and the Channel mattered because French fleets had to pass through its operating area. A long detour would cost time and still leave the fleet open to interception. Accurate positioning could also encourage misplaced confidence if the available charts were poor.

evidence.note: GPS accuracy, unreliable charts, wind and currents, and the Western Squadron's position off Brest.

segments.summary: Even with modern positioning, wind, tides, currents, and chokepoints would still govern where Age of Sail fleets could fight.
segments.question: How much would GPS help a French Age of Sail fleet?
segments.answerShort: It would improve navigation, but it could not remove the constraints of wind, tide, current, and the routes fleets had to use.

segments.title: How the Orlando experience tightened naval engine procurement
segments.body: Early steam procurement drew on many firms producing relatively few engines, so the Navy often had to accept what suppliers could provide. After the Orlando problems, it became more willing to reject machinery that missed the required figures. Because the Royal Navy was Britain's dominant steam-engine customer for decades, those standards encouraged capable firms to expand and pushed weaker suppliers out of the market.

evidence.note: The Orlando experience linked to stricter engine acceptance and industrial consolidation.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy used its purchasing power to demand engines that met defined performance standards after the Orlando experience.
segments.question: Did the Royal Navy become stricter about shipyard and engine variations after the Orlando problems?
segments.answerShort: Yes, especially for machinery: engines increasingly had to meet specified performance, and the Navy's buying power reshaped the supplier market.

segments.title: What a surviving HMS Tiger might do in the Second World War
segments.body: HMS Tiger's survival would depend first on her condition and capacity for modernization. Her comparatively open design might accept 14-inch weapons, improved machinery, and stronger air defence, giving the Royal Navy another fast capital ship. She could hunt raiders in the South Atlantic, operate off Norway, or reinforce the Far East. In each case, her speed would make her more useful than an old slow battleship.

evidence.note: Tiger's reconstruction options and several plausible wartime stations.

segments.summary: A retained Tiger could be reconstructed and used for raider hunting, Norway, or distant-station reinforcement much like Renown.
segments.question: If HMS Tiger survived the treaty period, how might the Royal Navy modernize and employ her in the Second World War?
segments.answerShort: She could receive a major reconstruction and serve as another fast capital ship for raider hunting, Norway, the South Atlantic, or the Far East.

segments.title: Why staff service did not guarantee a plum naval appointment
segments.body: Staff work did not create an automatic path to a broad pennant. A returning captain's prospects depended on his performance, the conventions of the period, and his political connections. A commodore appointment could be a reward or a useful employment without becoming an entitlement. It remained a temporary command appointment rather than a change in the officer's substantive Royal Navy rank.

evidence.note: The result depends on performance, era, and political alignment rather than following automatically from staff work.

segments.summary: War Office or Admiralty work might help a captain obtain a desirable command, but performance, period, and political connections still governed the outcome.
segments.question: Would War Office or Admiralty service normally earn a returning captain a plum appointment such as commodore?
segments.answerShort: It might, but only depending on his performance, the period, and his political connections; no appointment was automatic.

segments.title: How the Formidables combined earlier battleship designs
segments.body: British pre-dreadnoughts show how much armament and mounting arrangements could change during a design's development. Some classes began with open mounts and ended with turrets. The Formidables are interpreted here as combining the preferred Majestic design with the Canopus class's better machinery and armour. That mixture helps explain how a new class could emerge from earlier designs without every modification becoming a separate class.

evidence.note: Changes in British pre-dreadnought armament and the Majestic-Canopus interpretation of the Formidables.

segments.summary: British pre-dreadnought development included changes within classes and new designs combining features from earlier ships.

segments.title: Why British naval and army budgets are hard to compare
segments.body: The headline British Army budget did not include the cost of every imperial land force. The British Indian Army and other imperial formations sat outside that central figure even though they contributed to the wider military system. Royal Navy expenditure was much more centrally concentrated. Direct percentage comparisons can therefore exaggerate the difference between British sea and land spending.

evidence.note: Centralized naval funding compared with distributed imperial army expenditure.

segments.summary: Royal Navy spending was centrally visible, while imperial land forces were funded through several separate systems.
segments.question: How did Royal Navy spending compare with the British Army budget during the pre-1914 naval race?
segments.answerShort: The Navy's central budget was often larger, but the comparison is distorted because major imperial land forces were funded outside the British Army total.

segments.title: Why an Anglo-American naval race would emphasize technology
segments.body: Anglo-American naval competition repeatedly focused on the largest or most capable weapons rather than raw ship totals. That pattern points toward a technology race between Britain and the United States. France and Italy offer a more plausible contest between similarly sized fleets. Japan could challenge the United States, but a prolonged numerical race risked bankruptcy.

evidence.note: Anglo-American technology races compared with possible numerical races involving Japan or the Mediterranean powers.

segments.summary: Britain and the United States were more likely to compete over gun and ship quality than over raw fleet numbers.
segments.question: Which navies were most likely to enter a battleship numbers race?
segments.answerShort: Britain and America were more prone to technological competition; France and Italy were better matched for a numerical race, while Japan risked bankruptcy against the United States.

segments.title: Renown and Tiger against Scharnhorst and Gneisenau
segments.body: The two German ships could threaten an unmodified Tiger, while Renown's heavier guns could damage them in return. A hypothetical Leopard armed with 15-inch guns would change the balance further. With both British ships carrying that calibre, a few additional hits could disable or sink one or both opponents. German attempts to run away might also obscure their own firing positions. These are conditional possibilities, with the outcome dependent on manoeuvre and chance.

evidence.note: Relative armament, the hypothetical 15-inch Leopard alternative, German withdrawal, and uncertainty in the battle result.

segments.summary: The outcome turns on the hypothetical Tiger's armament and whether German attempts to escape interfere with their own fire.
segments.question: How might Renown and Tiger fare against Scharnhorst and Gneisenau?
segments.answerShort: The British pair could inflict severe damage, especially if both carried 15-inch guns, but the result would depend on hits, German manoeuvres, and luck.

segments.title: Why no-retreat simulations exaggerate naval battle losses
segments.body: A naval commander can break off an action once it is going badly. The standalone simulations discussed here force both sides to keep fighting, so they produce more decisive losses than a real encounter would necessarily cause. The campaign does allow ships to run away. That distinction matters when using a game result to estimate what historical captains would have risked.

evidence.note: Forced combat in standalone scenarios compared with real commanders withdrawing.
The later correction distinguishes campaign withdrawal from standalone simulations.

segments.summary: Standalone Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts simulations exaggerate losses when neither side can withdraw; the campaign permits escape.

segments.title: How more retained capital ships reshape the Royal Navy in 1939
segments.body: Fourteen 15-inch battleships, Nelson and Rodney, and four battlecruisers would give the Royal Navy twenty capital ships before the King George V class arrived. That force would strengthen the case for faster Nelsons and more extensive Queen Elizabeth reconstructions. Several battle squadrons could cover home waters and the Mediterranean while battlecruisers moved among the Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Indian Ocean. Wider coverage would increase the chance that German surface raiders met a British capital ship early in the war.

evidence.note: Estimate of the enlarged capital fleet, likely modernization priorities, squadron organization, and raider-hunting effects.

segments.summary: Retaining more Revenges and battlecruisers could support several battle squadrons and wider raider-hunting coverage at the start of war.
segments.question: How would eight Revenge-class ships and additional retained battlecruisers affect the Royal Navy by 1939?
segments.answerShort: They would provide enough capital ships for several battle squadrons and wider fast-ship deployments, while encouraging faster reconstructions and fast Nelson-class designs.

segments.title: The component evidence behind an 18-inch Agincourt hypothesis
segments.body: The Royal Navy already had 13.5-inch weapons available, while the known 15-inch turrets can be traced to the R-class program rather than to Agincourt. Small-tube boilers and geared turbines do appear where the Agincourt project can plausibly explain their development. An 18-inch gun program also emerges in the right period without another matching battleship project. The case rests on component provenance and timing. It remains an inference rather than a settled reconstruction of the ship.

evidence.note: Available gun sizes, R-class turret orders, machinery developments, and the otherwise unexplained 18-inch-gun program.

segments.summary: An 18-inch-gun Agincourt remains a hypothesis based on machinery and gun-program timing.

segments.title: When 28 knots counted as fast for a battleship
segments.body: Speed labels are historical categories rather than absolute ones. A 28-knot battleship sits at the entry point for a fast battleship in the 1920s and 1930s, while later designs pushed the category higher. The same speed can imply different operational roles in different design generations. Interwar ships should therefore be judged against contemporary fleets rather than their faster successors.

evidence.note: About 28 knots as the entry threshold for a fast battleship in the 1920s and 1930s.

segments.summary: A battleship's speed category depends on its period, with about 28 knots marking the fast-battleship threshold in the 1920s and 1930s.
segments.question: Would a 28-knot battleship count as a fast battleship?
segments.answerShort: Yes for the 1920s and 1930s: about 28 knots is the entry point, although later fast battleships were quicker.

segments.title: HMS Africa's solitary approach at Trafalgar
segments.body: HMS Africa entered Trafalgar as a third British column by herself. That one-ship column is the reason for selecting Africa in this short comparison of ships with distinctive histories.

evidence.note: Africa as the preferred example, forming a third Trafalgar column by herself.

segments.summary: HMS Africa's individual approach effectively created a one-ship third British column at Trafalgar.

segments.title: Why a Type 22 needed either missiles or a gun
segments.body: Batch 1 Type 22 frigates carried Exocet without a 4.5-inch gun. Their armament demonstrates that the Royal Navy accepted missiles in place of a medium gun. Removing Exocet as well would probably make the proposed armament unacceptable. The later Type 22 design changed the arrangement again.

evidence.note: The hypothetical omission of both Exocet and the medium gun, contrasted with the accepted missile-armed Batch 1 Type 22.

segments.summary: Exocet made a gunless Batch 1 Type 22 acceptable, but omitting both forms of surface armament would be a different proposition.
segments.question: Would the Royal Navy accept a Type 22 frigate with neither Exocet nor a 4.5-inch gun?
segments.answerShort: Probably not. Batch 1 Type 22s omitted the gun because they carried Exocet; removing both would go too far.

segments.title: Why moving a capital-ship turret changes the whole design
segments.body: A battlecruiser derived from the Queen Elizabeth design could delete a turret to create machinery space, but it could not casually move that turret elsewhere. Relocating a heavy turret forces major structural and internal rearrangement. Those changes propagate through the hull form and turn the proposal into a substantially new ship. Gun layouts cannot be separated from machinery and structural design. The scale of the redesign also explains why the Royal Navy might treat the result as a new class rather than an ordinary variant.

evidence.note: Why shifting a turret would require redesigning the ship and changing the form inherited from the Queen Elizabeth class.

segments.summary: Changing a Queen Elizabeth-derived turret arrangement would alter internal volume and hull form enough to undermine the premise of a simple class variant.
segments.question: Could a Queen Elizabeth-derived battlecruiser move a turret from the after position to an amidships position?
segments.answerShort: Not as a simple variant: moving the turret would force a redesign of the ship's internal arrangement and hull form.

segments.title: How a gun deck shifted between combat and daily life
segments.body: Tables and benches occupied the gun deck during ordinary shipboard life. Sailors used them for eating and for making or mending equipment. The furniture was put away when the crew worked the guns. Living and working arrangements therefore changed when the deck needed to function as a fighting space.

evidence.note: When gun-deck tables and benches were cleared and the everyday work they supported when in place.

segments.summary: Tables and benches on a sailing warship's gun deck were moved to clear the guns, then returned for eating and everyday work.

segments.title: How sensitive performance data limits modern naval war games
segments.body: Naval war games have historically drawn on intelligence estimates of real weapon and sensor performance. Public leaks and tighter protection of sensitive specifications make that practice harder to discuss openly. Exercises may still use informed estimates, but participants should expect important values and assumptions to be limited, altered, or withheld. A public ruleset cannot be assumed to reproduce operational capabilities faithfully.

evidence.note: Commercial war-game rules, intelligence estimates, and protection of real system capabilities.

segments.summary: Commercial rules can support professional exercises, but real capability estimates remain sensitive and may be deliberately constrained.
segments.question: Can professional naval war games use commercial rules with accurate performance data for the systems?
segments.answerShort: They can use commercial frameworks, but real performance estimates are sensitive and may be altered or withheld even when intelligence-informed assumptions are used.

segments.title: What replaces Exocet if it is unavailable?
segments.body: Harpoon is the suggested alternative if Exocet is unavailable. Its 1977 entry into service makes it a candidate for earlier Royal Navy adoption in this counterfactual. Older anti-ship missiles could also remain available to other operators. Air-defence missiles provide another surface-attack option, with Sea Dart given as an example.

evidence.note: Harpoon's 1977 service entry, possible earlier adoption, older missiles, and Sea Dart's secondary anti-ship role.

segments.summary: A no-Exocet counterfactual puts greater weight on Harpoon and other missiles capable of attacking ships.
segments.question: What changes if Exocet is unavailable?
segments.answerShort: Harpoon would play a larger role, alongside older anti-ship missiles and the surface-attack capabilities of air-defence missiles.

segments.title: A guide to the steam battleship's emergence
segments.body: Andrew Lambert's Battleships in Transition covers 1815 to 1860, from the end of the Napoleonic Wars to the launch of HMS Warrior. The book connects the design history of steam line-of-battle ships to the strategic and political decisions of the Crimean War. Britain needed steam battleships in more than one theatre but had too few completed ships to meet every demand. That shortage makes the transition from sail to steam a problem of strategy and procurement as well as technology.

evidence.note: Battleships in Transition; its chronological scope.
Steam line-of-battle ships, gaps in earlier research, and their influence on Crimean War strategy and procurement.

segments.summary: Andrew Lambert's Battleships in Transition is recommended for understanding how fleets moved from the Napoleonic era toward steam battleships.

segments.title: How a Type 22 without anti-ship missiles would be armed
segments.body: The gun was omitted because anti-ship missiles were expected to take over its surface-combat role. Without those missiles, the Royal Navy would put a gun on the design. The Type 42 provides the comparison because it did carry one. The separate political claim about cancellation goes beyond that design choice: harmful results from poor funding and defence organization do not by themselves establish an intention to weaken the country.

evidence.note: A gun as the alternative to anti-ship missiles, the Type 42 comparison, and the distinction between poor defence management and deliberate national weakening.

segments.summary: A Type 22 without anti-ship missiles would retain a gun for surface combat, as Type 42 destroyers did.
segments.question: Would a Type 22 without anti-ship missiles be rejected and cancelled as part of a deliberate weakening of British defence?
segments.answerShort: The Navy would fit a gun instead. The criticism concerns poor funding and defence organization; the claim of a deliberate plan to weaken Britain is rejected.

segments.title: Why steamship scarcity forced mixed Crimean War fleets
segments.body: The crisis with Russia required the Royal Navy to cover two widely separated fleets. The Mediterranean fleet's second-in-command insisted on the steam battleship Agamemnon as his flagship, yet the Mediterranean force could field only two British steam battleships against three French ones. Napier received most of Britain's available steam line-of-battle ships for the Baltic, but still took six sailing battleships, while the French contribution there was also largely sail. Russian fleets remained protected behind major fortresses, so the new steam battleships never received the open fleet action that might have proved their value. Scarce hulls and competing theatre priorities required steam and sailing battleships to serve together.

evidence.note: Steamship shortages, theatre allocations, mixed Allied fleets, and Russian fleets sheltering behind fortresses.

segments.summary: Britain needed steam battleships in both the Baltic and Black Sea, but too few existed to avoid mixed fleets of steam and sailing ships.

segments.title: Emergency conversions for Russia, new battleships for France
segments.body: Surveyor Baldwin Walker converted available 80-gun ships, including completed and unfinished hulls, because they could enter service sooner against Russia. He did not regard those ships as the ideal foundation of the future steam battle fleet. Walker and First Lord James Graham expected France to resume its place as Britain's principal naval rival after the war, so they continued larger new construction for that contest. Victoria, Howe, and Revenge belonged to this longer-term programme. Victoria and Howe took more than five years to build because Walker insisted on the quality of their materials.

evidence.note: Hurried 80-gun conversions for war with Russia and larger new construction against the expected French threat.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy converted available 80-gun ships for immediate war service while reserving first-rate new construction for the longer-term French challenge.

segments.title: How political support shaped Walker's steam-fleet programme
segments.body: Graham's departure from the Admiralty in February 1855 removed Walker's strongest political ally. Charles Wood lacked Graham's understanding of naval affairs and political influence, and no fresh construction followed the ships already building. Attention shifted to the immediate war effort, especially the Crimea. Walker nevertheless retained considerable departmental freedom, including direct wartime orders to dockyards without referring them through the Admiralty.

evidence.note: Graham's departure, Wood's different priorities, the pause in further construction, and Walker's direct authority over wartime dockyard work.

segments.summary: Graham's replacement by Charles Wood interrupted further construction, although Walker retained authority to direct wartime dockyard work.

segments.title: How Baltic bombardment needs secured new small craft
segments.body: Graham resisted spending on craft needed for the current war while accepting expensive battleships intended for a future conflict with France. Napier's request for gunboats and mortar vessels brought advice to hire Swedish steamers, and the Admiralty improvised gunboats from old steam packets. One of those makeshift vessels blew up. The Baltic bombardment requirement eventually led to a force of floating batteries, blockships, gunboats, and mortar vessels alongside French support. Graham justified the £650,000 programme to Gladstone by pointing to its postwar usefulness for coastal defence.

evidence.note: Resistance to small-craft spending, improvised gunboats, the Baltic bombardment force, and its postwar coastal-defence justification.

segments.summary: A need for shallow-water bombardment craft finally overcame resistance to gunboat spending when the program was also justified for postwar coastal defence.

segments.title: Why missile confidence displaced dogfight training after Korea
segments.body: The doctrinal break came after the Korean War rather than during it. American planners expected air-to-air missiles and changing interception methods to prevent fighters from reaching close combat. Vietnam exposed the gap between that expectation and operational reality. The Navy's Top Gun school restored specialist training after combat showed that technology had not removed the need for dogfighting skill.

evidence.note: The post-Korea missile assumption distinguished from Vietnam's evidence and the later creation of Top Gun training.

segments.summary: The United States reduced dogfight training because it expected missiles to make close air combat obsolete, not because Korea had disproved dogfighting.
segments.question: Did the United States abandon dogfight training because of its Korean War experience?
segments.answerShort: No. It expected missiles to end close air combat after Korea, but Vietnam disproved that assumption and helped bring specialist dogfight training back.

segments.title: How steamships managed coal soot on their sails
segments.body: Funnel smoke deposited soot on the rig of ships that combined steam and sail. When steaming, the sails were normally furled so exhaust could rise without a full spread of canvas in its path. The cloth could still become dirty, but routine cleaning dealt with the residue. Hybrid operation created extra maintenance without making the sailing rig unusable.

evidence.note: Coal soot accumulating on the sails of ships with both steam and sail.
The sails were furled under steam, could get dirty, and were cleaned.

segments.summary: Coal smoke dirtied the sails of ships that combined steam and sail, but crews managed the problem by furling and cleaning them.
segments.question: Did coal smoke foul the sails of ships that combined steam and sail?
segments.answerShort: Yes, but sails were furled when steaming so smoke could escape, and crews could clean the soot afterward.

segments.title: How turboprop success in Korea might alter British naval aviation
segments.body: A more successful Korean air war could change British judgements about air defence. If turboprop aircraft shot down more jets, their continued value would be harder to dismiss. That result might slow changes in Britain's approach to air defence. The Royal Navy's assessment of its own turboprop aircraft could also change.

evidence.note: Greater turboprop success against jets in Korea linked to slower British air-defence change and different Royal Navy aircraft decisions.

segments.summary: A Korean air war in which turboprops killed more jets could slow British movement toward new air-defence assumptions and change Royal Navy aircraft choices.
segments.question: How might a more successful turboprop air war in Korea affect British naval aviation?
segments.answerShort: It could slow Britain's shift toward new air-defence assumptions and make the Royal Navy reassess the value of its turboprop aircraft.

segments.title: The fire that destroyed HMS Glasgow at Montego Bay
segments.body: The 1779 loss of the 20-gun HMS Glasgow began when a steward stealing rum dropped a light onto a cask. Her gunpowder cargo put the ship, nearby vessels, and Montego Bay at risk. Captain Thomas Lloyd, Lieutenant Richard Oakley, and the crew fought the fire, removed the powder, and evacuated about 160 men before the burning ship was hauled clear. The master died from his injuries the next morning; another sailor died nine days later, although the connection with the fire is uncertain. Glasgow had earlier escaped six Continental Navy vessels on her maiden voyage, so the fire ended the career of a ship that had already survived a remarkable action.

evidence.note: The fire aboard Glasgow and the danger from her gunpowder cargo.
Lloyd's command, Oakley's response, powder removal, evacuation, casualties, and Nelson's contemporary testimony.
Glasgow's loss in 1779 at Montego Bay and her earlier escape from Continental Navy ships.

segments.summary: A rum theft started the 1779 fire aboard HMS Glasgow, while the crew's effort to remove the powder prevented a wider disaster at Montego Bay.

segments.title: How Nelson's testimony corrects the HMS Glasgow rescue story
segments.body: Later biographers Clarke and McArthur made Nelson the central figure in the rescue of HMS Glasgow, displacing Captain Thomas Lloyd, Lieutenant Richard Oakley, and the crew. Nelson's own evidence to the court martial presents a different picture: Lloyd encouraged his men, the crew formed a line to fight the fire, and the powder was removed before evacuation. Nelson did provide boats and help carry survivors to Badger, so his contribution was real. The dispute concerns the scale of his role and who received credit. Comparing the heroic biography with contemporary testimony shows how a famous reputation can distort the record of a shipboard emergency.

evidence.note: Clarke and McArthur's heroic account compared with Lloyd's, Oakley's, and the crew's actions.
Nelson's court-martial statement credits Lloyd and the crew and describes the evacuation, later casualties, and Lloyd's subsequent career.

segments.summary: Nelson's own court-martial statement credits Captain Thomas Lloyd and HMS Glasgow's crew, undercutting later biographies that made Nelson the sole rescuer.

segments.title: Why Nelson's promotion to post-captain at twenty mattered
segments.body: Peter Parker arranged a frigate command for Nelson and promoted him to post-captain. Nelson left Badger in Collingwood's hands on 20 June. He was only twenty when he secured his place on the captains' list. That early entry gave him time for the long progression toward flag rank.

evidence.note: Parker's frigate appointment, Badger's transfer to Collingwood, and Nelson's age and prospects on entering the captains' list.

segments.summary: A frigate appointment put the twenty-year-old Nelson on the captains' list and left him time to advance toward flag rank.

segments.title: Why a better MiG-15 engine might arrive too late
segments.body: More research into axial-flow compressors could have produced a better Soviet engine. It could also have taken longer, leaving that engine unavailable when the MiG-15 needed it. Improved performance would therefore have to be weighed against the development schedule.

evidence.note: Axial-flow research might improve the engine but could also delay it until it was unavailable in time.

segments.summary: More Soviet work on axial-flow compressors might improve the MiG-15's engine, but the extra development could also delay it beyond the moment when it was needed.
segments.question: Would more Soviet work on axial-flow compressors necessarily give the MiG-15 a better engine in time?
segments.answerShort: Possibly not: the engine might improve, but the extra development could delay it until after the period when it was needed.

segments.title: Naval conspiracy claims and a proposed Mary Celeste explanation
segments.body: A story that Tsushima's Russian sailors handed over their ships and retired to Hawaii is dismissed as nonsense. Contentious issues in naval history do not automatically imply a hidden plot. For Mary Celeste, the proposed explanation is that unfamiliar cargo noises made the crew fear an explosion and leave the ship. Their connection to the vessel could then have been lost when the boat line parted.

evidence.note: Contentious history distinguished from unsupported conspiracy stories.
Cargo fears and a parted boat line as a proposed explanation for Mary Celeste's abandonment.

segments.summary: The Tsushima conspiracy story is rejected, while cargo fears and a parted boat line offer a proposed explanation for Mary Celeste's abandonment.
segments.question: Which naval conspiracy theory is most plausible, and which is the worst misreading of the evidence?
segments.answerShort: The Tsushima story is dismissed as baseless. Cargo fears followed by a parted boat line offer a proposed explanation for Mary Celeste's abandonment.

segments.title: Use battle honours to find a naval story worth pursuing
segments.body: David Thomas's Battles and Honours of the Royal Navy separates awarded campaign honours, actions without honours, single-ship and boat actions, Fleet Air Arm squadron honours, and Royal Marine awards. Battles appear in alphabetical order, so a reader can look up an action and find the participating ships. Short entries connect names and dates to operational accounts, including Hermione's recovery and the naval contribution at San Sebastián. The book also records actions for which no honour was awarded.

evidence.note: Battles and Honours of the Royal Navy; its sections.
Squadron honours, the Hermione action, and alphabetical battle entries.

segments.summary: David Thomas's battles-and-honours reference lets readers work from a ship, squadron, or campaign name to the action behind it.

segments.title: Fleet Air Arm honours connect successive wars
segments.body: A naval air squadron's honours can span very different campaigns. The entries for 800, 801, and 809 Naval Air Squadrons include operations in Norway, the Mediterranean, Malta convoys, the Arctic, and the war against Japan. Later honours extend the same institutional line into Korea and the Falkland Islands. Together, these honours trace Fleet Air Arm service across aircraft generations and wars.

evidence.note: The campaign honours of 809, 801, and 800 Naval Air Squadrons across the Second World War, Korea, and the Falklands.

segments.summary: The honours of 800, 801, and 809 Naval Air Squadrons trace Fleet Air Arm service from the Second World War through Korea and the Falklands.

segments.title: HMS Surprise recaptures Hermione at Puerto Cabello
segments.body: Hermione's crew had handed the ship to Spain in 1797. Two years later she lay at Puerto Cabello with 385 men aboard, between two shore batteries. Captain Hamilton attacked with HMS Surprise and recovered the ship after fierce fighting. The casualty figures given are 119 Spanish dead and 97 wounded against twelve British wounded.

evidence.note: Hermione's transfer to Spain, Puerto Cabello's defences, Hamilton's attack, and reported casualty figures.

segments.summary: Captain Edward Hamilton's HMS Surprise recovered the former HMS Hermione from Spanish service in a cutting-out action at Puerto Cabello in 1799.

segments.title: How an ice-free Arctic changes Age of Sail strategy
segments.body: An ice-free Arctic would put Russia in a much more difficult strategic position. Open water along the coasts would give British forces routes and operational choices unavailable in the historical climate, including access toward the Pacific. Those routes would change the approaches that Russia would have to defend and the directions from which British sailing fleets could operate.

evidence.note: Russian vulnerability and Pacific access in an ice-free Arctic.

segments.summary: Reliable Arctic passages would expose Russian approaches and create new Pacific routes for British sailing fleets.
segments.question: What might the Royal Navy have done if the Arctic had been reliably ice-free in the Age of Sail?
segments.answerShort: It would gain new routes against Russia and toward the Pacific, substantially changing the strategic geography of northern waters.

segments.title: San Sebastián honours reveal naval support ashore
segments.body: Sir George Collier's squadron first removed a hard-pressed British garrison from the Santander area and carried it to safety. The ships then cooperated with General Thomas Graham during the reduction of San Sebastián. A weeks-long blockade helped isolate the French-held town until its surrender in September 1813. The reference distinguishes ships awarded the honour from additional vessels and gunboats mentioned in dispatches. The contribution of those additional craft is unclear.

evidence.note: Collier's troop evacuation, cooperation with General Graham, the blockade and surrender, and the ships awarded honours or mentioned in dispatches.

segments.summary: In 1813, Collier's squadron evacuated troops, supported General Graham, and blockaded the French-held town of San Sebastián.

segments.title: How many extra Scharnhorsts could replace Bismarck and Tirpitz
segments.body: Four to six additional Scharnhorst-type ships is the rough estimate for redirecting the effort spent on Bismarck and Tirpitz. The estimate concerns the available construction time and resources, without a detailed shipyard schedule.

evidence.note: Estimate of four to six additional ships in place of Bismarck and Tirpitz.

segments.summary: Redirecting the Bismarck-class effort might produce four to six additional Scharnhorst-type ships in the available time.
segments.question: How many additional Scharnhorst-class ships might Germany have built instead of Bismarck and Tirpitz?
segments.answerShort: Roughly four to six additional ships, given the time and resources available.

segments.title: How machinery conversion could extend Type 82 service
segments.body: The Type 82's combined steam-and-gas machinery left a possible route to modernization. The steam installation could be replaced by a second gas plant if the ships underwent a sufficiently extensive conversion. There was also internal space for upgrades. No service-life estimate is given, because the answer depends on how much rebuilding the class receives.

evidence.note: Possible replacement of the steam installation with another gas plant, with space available for upgrades.

segments.summary: A larger Type 82 class could gain service life through machinery replacement and other upgrades, depending on the extent of conversion.
segments.question: How long could eight Type 82 destroyers remain in service, given their steam machinery?
segments.answerShort: Their service life would depend on the extent of modernization. Replacing the steam installation with a second gas plant could extend it.

segments.title: What would replace hypothetical Type 82 losses in the Falklands?
segments.body: The hypothetical fleet could contain eight Type 82s alongside eight Type 42s. Losses in the Falklands would then force a choice about which design to order as replacements. Type 42s could replace lost Type 82s if Type 42 was the ship still in production. More Type 82s would also remain an option if their production continued.

evidence.note: Replacement choices after hypothetical Falklands losses, conditional on which destroyer designs remained in production.

segments.summary: Falklands losses would test which destroyer design remained available to build in a hypothetical mixed Type 82 and Type 42 fleet.
segments.question: How would a mixed Type 82 and Type 42 fleet affect the choice between quality and quantity after Falklands losses?
segments.answerShort: Replacement orders would depend on which ships were lost and whether both designs remained in production.

segments.title: How piracy endangered English trade with the Mughal Empire
segments.body: English pirates operating from American colonies targeted Indian Ocean trade while the East India Company depended on Mughal permission to trade. Henry Every's seizure of the Mughal emperor's ship in 1695 forced the Company to undertake escorts for Mughal shipping to recover its privileges. William Kidd's later capture of an Indian merchant ship deepened the crisis. Colonial officials and political interests had helped shelter piracy, while the Dutch VOC encouraged Mughal suspicion of English traders. By 1701, piracy had endangered the Company's position and become an embarrassment to its political supporters.

evidence.note: American colonial support for piracy, Mughal retaliation, the escort obligation after Every's raid, and Kidd's capture and prosecution.

segments.summary: Indian Ocean piracy exposed the East India Company to Mughal retaliation and forced it to protect shipping attacked by other Englishmen.

segments.title: How William III's accession weakened the East India Company's position
segments.body: William III's accession forced the East India Company into an uneasy alliance with its commercial rival, the Dutch VOC. At home, the Company's close association with James II also damaged its position. The VOC carried much of the fighting against French establishments in India, but Whig support for rival traders challenged the English Company's monopoly. A new company formed in 1698 to take over its patent.

evidence.note: The forced VOC alliance, the Company's ties to James II, Whig support for competitors, and the new company of 1698.

segments.summary: Dynastic change exposed the East India Company to a difficult Dutch alliance and political support for competitors at home.

segments.title: How domestic politics narrowed English strategy before 1701
segments.body: Financial exhaustion ended the previous war in 1697 without removing Louis XIV's ambitions or the approaching Spanish succession crisis. English politicians nevertheless disbanded most of the army and viewed foreign affairs mainly through domestic disputes. Commercial interests still sent Anglo-Dutch fleets into the Baltic, where they acted with Sweden and bombarded Copenhagen, while illegal trade and the Darien colony poisoned relations with Spain in the Caribbean. The Act of Settlement then required parliamentary consent for European war, barred foreign-born officeholders, and constrained the monarch's travel. Overseas commitments continued to demand naval action while Parliament restricted William III's freedom of action.

evidence.note: The 1697 peace, Caribbean and Baltic interests, Copenhagen's bombardment, and parliamentary restrictions on William III.

segments.summary: After the Peace of Ryswick, English domestic politics constrained William III even as Caribbean, Baltic, and Spanish succession problems kept demanding maritime attention.

segments.title: How Louis XIV provoked another coalition over the Spanish succession
segments.body: The European powers had negotiated a division of Spain's empire because none wanted another war. Charles II's will instead left his possessions to the Duke of Anjou, and Louis XIV accepted it in place of the treaties. French troops then entered the Spanish Netherlands, higher tariffs threatened foreign trade, and French officials tried to control access to Spanish America. These actions threatened Dutch security and English and Dutch commerce. Louis's recognition of James II's son after his father's death in 1701 added a direct challenge to England's settlement.

evidence.note: Partition treaties, Charles II's will, French military and commercial moves, and recognition of James II's son.

segments.summary: French moves over Spain's inheritance threatened Dutch security and Anglo-Dutch commerce, then challenged England's royal succession.

segments.title: Why French silver convoys needed large escort squadrons
segments.body: Allied strategy aimed to interrupt Spain's Atlantic connections and open Spanish American trade, while control of the western Mediterranean would separate Spain from its Italian possessions and support Savoy. Spain's weak navy made French escorts necessary for returning American silver. Spanish governors nevertheless distrusted French interference and wanted the silver landed in Spain, fearing that little would return if it went to France. A few fast ships might have carried the silver more safely on military grounds. Large escort squadrons served a political purpose by demonstrating French commitment and overcoming Spanish resistance.

evidence.note: Allied maritime strategy, Spanish dependence on French escorts, distrust over the destination of silver, and the political case for large squadrons.

segments.summary: French escorts protected Spanish silver while confronting Spanish distrust, making squadron size a political choice as well as a military one.

segments.title: Command of the Ocean as a broad guide to naval history
segments.body: Command of the Ocean offers a broad account of naval history for its period. It gives readers an overview of the subjects they will encounter while also providing substantial detail. A reader seeking greater depth on one question can use that foundation before turning to specialist works.

evidence.note: Command of the Ocean recommended for broad coverage while allowing for more detailed reading on individual subjects.

segments.summary: Command of the Ocean is recommended as a broad foundation for the political, commercial, and operational context of naval history.

segments.title: The Brest blockade beyond the famous fleet actions
segments.body: The study of the Brest blockade follows the work required to keep the Channel Fleet off the French port from 1793 to 1815. Its 1797 example contrasts the victories at Cape St Vincent and Camperdown with the sustained work of watching the French fleet, protecting trade, assembling forces, and avoiding weather that could drive the blockaders too far west. Orders, supply problems, and frigate shortages reveal the resources needed to keep the blockade operating. The later dispute between Bridport and Pellew adds professional rivalry and prize money to that command problem.

evidence.note: The Brest blockade book; the 1797 orders and operational problems.
Provisioning rotations, ship wear, intelligence reports, and frigate shortages.
Evidence surrounding Bridport, Pellew, and prize money.

segments.summary: A detailed study of the 1793-1815 Brest blockade shows that keeping a fleet on station was a continuing command and endurance problem.

segments.title: Lord Keith's request for an English peerage
segments.body: After his efforts to bring the Nore mutiny under control, Lord Keith asked Spencer for an English peerage in addition to his Irish title. Spencer acknowledged the favourable impression his service had made on the king but deferred the prospect of a further honour. Keith's earlier career included the capture of Charleston, service at Toulon and its evacuation, and command of the squadron that seized the Cape of Good Hope. Parliamentary service also helped him establish political connections. His political connections included Pitt, Spencer and Henry Dundas.

evidence.note: Keith's request and Spencer's reply, followed by his operational career and political connections.

segments.summary: Keith's request for another peerage places his handling of the Nore mutiny alongside earlier commands and political connections.

segments.title: The rotation and intelligence behind the Brest blockade
segments.body: The Admiralty worried about supply and the cumulative wear on ships kept off Brest. Rather than return the entire fleet to Torbay, it considered sending ships into nearby anchorages two at a time for provisions. Reports from a frigate captain and an escaped British sailor indicated nineteen French ships of the line, additional frigates, and tens of thousands of troops assembling for a possible expedition to Ireland. Bridport simultaneously complained that too few frigates were available to watch and communicate. Maintaining the blockade depended on provisioning ships without opening a gap in the watch and on obtaining reliable reports of French preparations.

evidence.note: Provisioning rotations, ship wear, French fleet and troop reports, and the shortage of frigates.

segments.summary: Keeping the Channel Fleet off Brest required rotating ships for provisions, finding enough frigates, and interpreting reports of French preparations.

segments.title: Why experienced captains stayed in frigate commands
segments.body: Bridport objected that Warren and Pellew remained in frigate commands despite their seniority. First Lord Spencer answered that the service they performed required their particular experience and ability. Warren eventually accepted the 74-gun Canada, but Pellew declined an offered ship of the line and chose to continue with his frigate squadron. His highly flattering refusal also exposes the careful language needed when rejecting a commander-in-chief's preferred career path. Specialist experience could justify keeping a senior captain in a frigate instead of assigning him a ship of the line.

evidence.note: Bridport's objection, Spencer's defence of the frigate captains, Warren's move to Canada, and Pellew's refusal.

segments.summary: The Admiralty kept senior captains such as John Borlase Warren and Edward Pellew in specialist frigate work because their experience outweighed a conventional move to ships of the line.

segments.title: Prize money and the Bridport-Pellew dispute
segments.body: Independent frigate commands kept captures outside the commander-in-chief's normal share, giving Bridport a financial reason to resent Pellew's freedom. Pellew himself accumulated a very large fortune in prize and freight money, although one biographer interprets his behaviour as fear of returning to poverty rather than simple greed. Writers also accused Bridport of avarice, drawing on his prize-money disputes and two wealthy marriages. Evidence complicating the charge against Bridport includes the settlement that protected his first wife's fortune and the limited conclusions that can be drawn from a disputed prize-money claim. Financial incentives alone do not establish that greed governed either man's conduct.

evidence.note: Prize-money rules and rival interpretations of Pellew's and Bridport's motives, including evidence against treating Bridport's marriages as fortune hunting.

segments.summary: Prize-money rules help explain hostility between Bridport and Pellew, but competing biographies warn against treating personal greed as a settled motive.

segments.title: Follow a Royal Navy ship name across centuries
segments.body: Ships of the Royal Navy collects vessels under the names they carried. HMS Thrasher runs from a small gunbrig to a nineteenth-century gunboat, a destroyer, and a T-class submarine. HMS Ardent leads through several eras, including Jutland, Norway, and the Falklands. Hero likewise spans 74-gun sailing ships, a screw second rate, a turret ship, and a destroyer. Dates and vessel types distinguish successive ships sharing the same name.

evidence.note: Ships of the Royal Navy as the sixth book, with audience requests for ship-name lookups.
Thrasher and Ardent across successive Royal Navy vessels.
The Hero name across sailing ships of the line, a screw second rate, a turret ship, and a destroyer.

segments.summary: An interactive look-up session shows how a ship-name reference can trace repeated names across very different vessels and wars.

segments.title: When two Huron entries may describe the same schooner
segments.body: The first Huron listed was the American schooner Ohio, captured on the Canadian lakes in 1814. A second schooner entry may describe that same vessel rebuilt, rather than a separate ship. The reference leaves the identity uncertain. Later Huron entries move to Canadian destroyers, so even a compact name list requires attention to both distinct vessels and possible duplication.

evidence.note: The captured Ohio, uncertainty over whether another Huron entry is the same schooner rebuilt, and later Canadian destroyers.

segments.summary: Early Huron entries preserve uncertainty over a rebuilt schooner before the name continues through Canadian destroyers.

segments.title: Did any ships named Ardent survive to retirement?
segments.body: The reference lists eleven ships named Ardent, with very different fates. An earlier destroyer was sold in 1911, while later examples were lost at Jutland, off Norway and in the Falklands War. A planned A-class submarine was cancelled in 1945. The wooden ships generally fared better, apart from the one that exploded off Corsica in 1794, and an Australian patrol boat became a museum ship.

evidence.note: The eleven Ardent entries, including ships sold, preserved, cancelled and lost in war.

segments.summary: The Ardent entries include ships sold or preserved as well as those lost at Jutland, off Norway, and in the Falklands.
segments.question: Did any ships named Ardent survive long enough to be scrapped?
segments.answerShort: Yes. An earlier destroyer was sold in 1911, several wooden ships survived, and an Australian patrol boat became a museum ship.

segments.title: The brief use of Cromwell as a Royal Navy ship name
segments.body: A C-class destroyer carried the name Cromwell in 1946 before becoming Bergen in Norwegian service. The reference gives a June renaming followed by sale in July. The short interval suggests that the rename was connected with the transfer. This qualifies the initial assumption that Cromwell's association with regicide had prevented any Royal Navy use of the name.

evidence.note: Initial rejection of Cromwell followed by a C-class destroyer entry recording the 1946 renaming and sale as Bergen.
Norway confirmed as Bergen's receiving navy.

segments.summary: A reference lookup corrects the initial assumption that Cromwell's association with regicide prevented any Royal Navy use of the name.
segments.question: Was there ever a Royal Navy ship named Cromwell?
segments.answerShort: Yes. A C-class destroyer briefly carried the name in 1946 before transfer to Norway as Bergen.

segments.title: Why Royal Navy launch dates cluster in certain months
segments.body: The Barfleur entries show particular months recurring in Royal Navy launch records. The pattern is linked to the timing of government payments because yards needed confidence that funds were available before completing costly work. Launch dates can therefore preserve evidence about the financial rhythms behind naval construction. A reference-book list becomes a clue to how shipyards managed cash flow and completion schedules.

evidence.note: Recurring completion months linked to government payment timing and yard finances.

segments.summary: Repeated launch months in ship histories can reflect the timing of government payments and shipyard finance.

segments.title: The many Royal Navy ships named Antelope
segments.body: The first Antelope in the reference is a galleon built in 1546 and rebuilt in 1577 and 1618. Parliamentarian forces burned her in 1649. Later bearers of the name included a seventeenth-century warship, a sloop lost in a hurricane off Jamaica, an India-built brig, a paddle sloop, and a torpedo gunboat. The sequence continues through destroyers to the Type 21 frigate. The repeated name spans changes in hulls, propulsion, and weapons, so dates and vessel types are essential to identifying the right ship.

evidence.note: The Antelope entries from the Tudor galleon through sailing, steam, destroyer, and Type 21 examples.

segments.summary: The name Antelope connects a Tudor galleon, sailing warships, small steam craft, destroyers, and the Type 21 frigate across four centuries.

segments.title: Was Swallow the Royal Navy's most reused ship name?
segments.body: The manual count finds 35 entries for Swallow or Swallow Prize, while the reference's note credits the name to 39 vessels, a dockyard craft, East India Company ships, and revenue cutters. The latest example identified became an Irish naval patrol vessel in the late twentieth century. These counts suggest Swallow was probably more frequently used than Falcon or Eagle. The conclusion remains qualified because the entries and the broader note count the name differently.

evidence.note: Swallow entries counted against the reference work's broader total for the name.

segments.summary: The reference-book count points to Swallow as one of the Royal Navy's most repeatedly used names across ships and smaller craft.
segments.question: What is the most commonly reused Royal Navy ship name?
segments.answerShort: Swallow is the strongest candidate, with the reference work crediting the name to 39 vessels plus several other naval and revenue craft.

segments.title: Using dynastic histories when a battle study is hard to obtain
segments.body: A dedicated study of the intended battle was difficult to find, while broader books discussed it. The research therefore turned to Cambridge histories of the Song dynasty and its successor. Because the battle belonged to the transition between dynasties, both histories were relevant.

evidence.note: Choice of Cambridge dynastic histories for a battle at the transition from the Song dynasty when a dedicated study was difficult to obtain.

segments.summary: Cambridge histories of the Song dynasty and its successor provide context when a dedicated battle study is difficult to obtain.

segments.title: Finding language help for research on Admiral Yi
segments.body: Research on Admiral Yi can encounter a language barrier when useful material is available in Korean. Korean students and other readers can help make that material accessible. Academic contacts offer another route to people with the required language skills. Alex Clarke offers to connect Drachinifel with a colleague teaching at a Korean university.

evidence.note: Question about Korean-language material on Admiral Yi and the suggestion of help from Korean students.
Offer to introduce Drachinifel to an academic contact teaching in Korea.

segments.summary: Korean readers and academic contacts offer ways to work with material on Admiral Yi that is otherwise inaccessible to a researcher.
segments.question: How can a historian research Admiral Yi when the available material is in Korean?
segments.answerShort: Seek help from Korean readers and academic contacts who can work with the material.

segments.title: Why a cork-filled battleship target did not need to sink
segments.body: Cork filling made the old battleship difficult to sink, but it did not make her literally unsinkable. The added resilience let the target survive repeated firing practice. Firing stopped once observers could establish that the target had been hit rather than after the ship was destroyed. The experiment therefore measured gunnery accuracy instead of terminal damage. Its success can only be judged against that test objective.

evidence.note: Cork made the target difficult to sink; firing stopped once hits were confirmed rather than after destruction.

segments.summary: Packing an old battleship with cork made it difficult to sink, but the exercise measured hits rather than destruction.
segments.question: Was the old battleship packed with cork successfully made into an unsinkable target?
segments.answerShort: Cork made the target very difficult to sink. The exercise measured confirmed hits, so firing did not have to continue until the ship was destroyed.
